runs.text: O que faz, ou cõcerta penas de Iapão.

lines.note: Fudeyui is a maker or repairer of writing brushes, connecting fude with yui, tying or binding. The y is visible after e and was omitted by OCR; the occupation follows naturally from the preceding page's brush entries.
Fudō means not moving, glossed ugokazu. The circumflex belongs to the word and is repeated in the example below.

runs.text: Não ſe mouer nem ſe mudar.

lines.note: Fudō fuhen means unmoving and unchanging. The Portuguese distinguishes movement from change, matching the two Japanese components.

runs.text: S. ¶ Item, Fudô, Nome de hum Fotoque.

lines.note: Fudō is also the name of a Buddhist deity. Both Fudô and Fotoque are italic in this Portuguese sentence; the mark over o has two sides and is a circumflex, not the OCR grave.
Shidai fudō describes an irregular or unordered sequence. The example starts with a printed capital X; this is distinct from the immobility sense of the preceding homograph.
The order lacks proportion and arrangement. Concerto is the historical arrangement/harmony word, not necessarily a musical concert.

runs.text: Inchaço que procede de ruim ar.

lines.note: Fūdokushu is a swelling attributed to bad air. This records the dictionary's medical explanation without treating it as modern medical guidance.
Fudō na means unequal or irregular, glossed onajikarazu. Restore the narrow i in deſigual; the Portuguese adjective agrees with the Japanese negative comparison.
Fudō na fushi, koe applies irregularity to a tune or voice. The two nouns are alternatives in the Japanese example, not additional headwords.
Disordered melody or voices translates the preceding example. The initial T belongs to the italic Portuguese word Toada, not a stray roman Japanese token.
Fudō ni is the adverbial form. Aduer. is an abbreviated editorial label and remains italic.
Fūha is wind and waves, expanded as kaze, nami. The following phrase concerns enduring this combination, hence weathering a storm.
Fūha wo shinogu means enduring wind and waves. The scan has n in xinogu, lost by OCR xiogu; the Portuguese suffering or passing through storms confirms the verb.
Fuhen here means unchanging, glossed kawarazu. The written-register S. is italic and the unmarked headword must not be confused with a differently accented reading.
Another fuhen is glossed amanekarazu, not universal or widespread. Its meaning differs from unchanging fuhen even though the romanized forms coincide.

runs.text: ſabido igualmente em todas as partes, ou não

lines.note: The definition concerns information not equally known in all places. The negative scope continues through this entire clause.

runs.text: terem todos a meſma noticia. S.

lines.note: Not everyone has the same knowledge or information. This completes the limited-diffusion sense of fuhen and is marked as written usage.
Fuhō is not conforming to law: nori narazu and hatto ni moruru supply the Japanese explanations. The source spells moruru and that historical form is retained.

runs.text: guardar a ley, ou não ſe lhe dar della.

lines.note: The lawlessness definition continues: failing to observe the law or caring nothing about it. The pronoun della refers back to ley.

runs.text: Couſa ſem ley, & ſem ordẽ. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Fuhō na is lawless or disorderly. The caron above o is visible, though faint; OCR omitted it. The adjective introduces a further personal application below.
A disorderly, lawless man is the additional sense of fuhō na, rather than an independent entry. The repeated Portuguese adjectives clarify the application to people.
Fūfu means husband and wife, expanded as otto and me. The initial V in Votto represents the historical spelling of the Japanese vowel, not a Portuguese consonant.

Fūfu kyōkai denotes the union of husband and wife. The first word repeats the preceding headword, and the scan shows the accented u rather than OCR Fafu; qeô is retained as the printed contracted-vowel spelling.
Wife completes the marital-union gloss from the previous row. This short physical line remains separately identifiable, despite belonging to the same sentence.
Fūga is explained as shīka no michi, the way of poetry. The historical Xijca spelling should not be normalized to a modern romanization; Portuguese identifies the activity as poetry and its art.
Composing verses completes the definition of the poetic art. This is ordinary Portuguese explanation, wholly italic, with no additional Japanese expression.

Fugainai describes lacking spirit or effectiveness. The historical sense is weakness or inability to carry something through, consistent with the modern Japanese adjective but not restricted to a modern evaluative translation.
Fugainai mono is a person lacking resolve or energy. The small final mark is a full stop, not a word-breaking hyphen; the Japanese phrase is complete before its Portuguese translation.

runs.text: Homem de poucos eſpiritos pera fazer, ou ſu-

lines.note: The example is translated as a man with little spirit for doing or sustaining something. Espiritos here concerns energy or courage, not supernatural beings.
Sustentar completes the verb split across the preceding row and this one: sustaining or upholding some undertaking. Preserve the physical break and its existing s-form evidence.

runs.text: Doença dos olhos que procede do ven-

lines.note: Fūgan is an eye disease attributed to wind or air. The accent over u is visibly an upward-opening caron, like nearby Fǔga, rather than the OCR circumflex.
Wind or air completes the historical etiological explanation of the eye disease. The line begins with the continuation of ven-to, not a separate Portuguese word.
Fugen means not decreasing, glossed herazu and otoroyezu. Both Japanese negatives concern diminution or deterioration; the Portuguese verb continues below.
Fuzō fugen means neither increasing nor decreasing. Empejorar is the historical word for worsening; do not replace it with a modern Portuguese synonym merely because its form resembles Spanish.
Neither growing nor diminishing translates fuzō fugen. The source's crecer and tilde position are retained rather than modernized.
Fugenzō names a variety of cherry tree. The initial letter of cereijeira is c, not the OCR e; the botanical gloss supports the recognizable Japanese cherry-variety name.
Fūgetsu, wind and moon, is written Fuguet with historical final t. Kaze and tsuki make the compound transparent; the terminal consonant is not an OCR truncation to be expanded in the diplomatic text.
Fūgi is custom or disposition, glossed katagi. The scan shows a caron over u, not a grave. Distinguish this accented word from the unaccented homographs that follow.
Fugi is a name for good wine or sake. The dictionary supplies no etymology here; the short definition should not be expanded into an unsupported identification of a particular drink.

Fugi means a fault or disorder, with a roman X. citation label. This physical row was absent from the saved OCR detector's sequence and needed its own manually placed crop; its stable ID is preserved.
Fugi wo kamayuru means behaving disobediently or improperly toward one's lord. The historical verb form kamayuru is retained; the phrase continues from Fu- on the preceding row.
Ill-mannered toward one's lord completes the translation of the example. Malcriado describes conduct here, not simply the literal circumstances of upbringing.
Fugi is explained as ha-ari, winged ants. Portuguese identifies ants that fly and supplies Agudeas as another name; preserve the printed space in fa ari.
Fugi na is culpable or faulty. This adjective returns to the moral-fault sense, not the intervening winged-ant homograph.
Fugi ni is the adverbial form associated with culpable conduct. Adu. is an italic grammatical abbreviation, not Japanese text.
Fugō means failing to agree or correspond, glossed awazu. The negative definition matters: it is not the positive modern compound for agreement merely inferred from the roman letters.
Another fugō is a damaged writing brush, literally kusare fude. The scan clearly includes f in fude, lost by OCR, and separates eſcreuer from ja. Its definition continues into column 2.

runs.text: nada, ou desfeita. Palaura de cartas em-

lines.note: The damaged or worn-out brush is a self-deprecating expression in letters. This is the continuation of column 1's last entry, not a new headword.

Fugō ni atawazu is an epistolary formula expressing that one's inadequate brush cannot do the matter justice. The first a is damaged, but the word is roman Japanese throughout; the OCR italic grave-accented à is not supported as a separate Portuguese token.

runs.text: Naõ ha pera que eſcreuer com eſta pena bota,

lines.note: The Portuguese paraphrase says there is no point writing with this blunt brush. Bota is an adjective meaning blunt here, not the noun for a boot.
Or damaged finishes the disparaging description of the writer's own brush. The short row belongs to the same epistolary example.
Fugōgo is inability, explained as gōgo sezu. The final Portuguese word is não, with visible o rather than OCR e; it begins a coordinated negative definition.

runs.text: ter faculdade pera fazer algũa couſa como pera

lines.note: Lacking the capacity to do something continues the definition. Faculdade here is ability or power, not an educational institution.

runs.text: eſcreuer, &c. ¶ Item, Não ſe poder bu

lines.note: Writing is an example of an activity one cannot perform. The additional sense concerns inability to move; bulir is split across rows without a clearly printed terminal hyphen here, so none is supplied.
Movement is prevented by old age or disability. Aleijão belongs to the historical wording; this note explains its function without endorsing its terminology for present-day use.
Fugōgo na hito is a person unable to act or move. Preserve the OCR's ligature transcription in Peßoa; the semantic reading does not require deciding its component s shapes anew.
Cannot move completes the definition of the person in the preceding Japanese example. The reflexive form mouerſe is historically unhyphenated in the printed text.
Fugu, explained as tsubusa narazu, means not being exhaustive or detailed. This is an epistolary expression rather than the fish of the same modern pronunciation.
Fugu tsutsushinde begins a deferential letter formula, completed by mōsu below. Portuguese diffuso means expansive or detailed in correspondence, not necessarily unclear.

runs.text: Não ſou mais diffuſo, ou não eſcre-

lines.note: Mōsu completes the Japanese formula. Portuguese diffuſo repeats the adjective of the preceding row; the scan has long s, not the OCR j that would make an anomalous word.
I do not write in detail completes the Portuguese paraphrase. The initial uo continues eſcre- from the previous physical row.
Fugu na means incomplete or deficient. The next example begins gotai, the body or its limbs, and is divided after Go- in print.
Gotai fugu na hito describes a person with a bodily impairment. The next Fu- starts another application of the same adjective, this time to a book.
Fugu na kyō is a book or scripture lacking leaves or gatherings. The Portuguese verb is faltão, with t rather than OCR i; it expresses exactly the material incompleteness in the Japanese adjective.
Gatherings or quires completes the account of an incomplete book. Quadernos refers to its physical units here, not an unrelated notebook entry.
Fuguri denotes male genital anatomy; the source uses the Latin euphemistic gloss Virga genitalis. Do not silently substitute a more precise modern anatomical term for the dictionary's wording.

Fūgai is outside accepted refinement or custom, expanded as fūryū fūzoku no hoka. The first accent is weak in the scan; the OCR grave-shaped transcription is retained pending firmer visual evidence rather than normalized solely from pronunciation.
Outside custom completes the gloss. The Japanese foca means hoka, outside; the source's cuſtume spelling is retained.

runs.text: Erua como de latada que dà flores.

lines.note: Fuji is the flowering climbing plant wisteria. The Portuguese describes its arbor-like growth; gi in this Japanese spelling represents the historical voiced palatal consonant, not modern hard g.
Fujibakama names a plant. The Portuguese begins Hũa, an indefinite feminine article, not OCR Pũa; the capital H is visible in the native crop.
Fūjin, literally wind and dust, denotes worldly occupations. The scan has Fǔgin without the extra OCR i; kaze and chiri identify the compound and prepare the figurative meaning below.
Fūjin ni magirete means being caught up in worldly affairs. The following isolated O is the beginning of Portuguese Ocupado, not an article to be joined to the Japanese phrase.

runs.text: cupado, ou embaraçado com negocios do mũdo.

lines.note: Occupied or entangled in worldly business translates magirete. Embaraçado concerns involvement or obstruction, not necessarily the modern English feeling of embarrassment.

runs.text: Hũa erua de latada, ou flor esten-

lines.note: Fujinami evokes spreading wisteria and its wave-like blossoms. The definition describes a climbing plant or extended flower mass rather than a separate aquatic object suggested by nami alone.
The flowers undulate in the wind. The italic P. marks poetic use, appropriate to the image of wisteria waves; it is an editorial label, not part of the Japanese expression.

runs.text: Certa laya de pano, como de linho

lines.note: Fujinuno is cloth made from the plant's fibre, compared with linen. Nuno is cloth; the botanical relationship to fuji explains the compound.
Made from this plant completes the material definition. The demonstrative points to the preceding wisteria entries, not to a newly named plant on this row.
Fujō means uncertainty or being unsettled, glossed sadamarazu. Retain the caron here; the following similarly spelled entry has a visibly different accent and a different gloss.
Fujō here concerns disorder or unrest, glossed totonowarazu. Portuguese narrows the application to sensual thoughts, continued below; the circumflex is clearly visible.
Fujō na mono is a person disturbed by sensual thoughts. Do not automatically replace this with the modern moral sense of impurity without attending to the dictionary's explicit explanation.
The Portuguese repeats the sensual-mental-disturbance sense for the example person. The text reaches the damaged right rule; the widened crop preserves the complete final word.
Fūjū is explained as kaze no naka, the midst of the air or wind. Meo is the source's historical spelling for the middle and is not expanded to modern meio.
Fuigo is a bellows used by a blacksmith or goldsmith. Foles is the Portuguese tool name and ouriues the historical spelling of the craft occupation.
Fuin is chastity or abstinence, explained negatively as tanoshimazu. The modern associations of enjoyment should not obscure the sexual restraint specified by the Portuguese definition.
Fuin ni suru or tamotsu means observing chastity. The alternate-verb marker l is not a Japanese consonant; the long s in suru is retained from the image-aligned OCR.

Fūja is harmful wind, glossed yokoshima no kaze. Enlargement shows a two-sided circumflex, not the OCR grave; retain that unusual printed accent rather than replacing it with the more usual u-caron. NINJAL independently records Fûja. The medical explanation continues below.

runs.text: netrou, ou que cauſou doença a alguem.

lines.note: Wind that entered the body or caused illness completes the historical explanation. The word is doença, with ç rather than OCR g; the visible cedilla and the meaning both support the correction.
Fuzei is appearance or manner. Ikari no fuzei supplies an expression of anger, preparing the action arawasu on the following row.
Ikari no fuzei wo arawasu means showing an angry appearance. The Portuguese concerns outward expression; the Japanese final verb matches that visible manifestation.
An exterior of annoyance completes the translation. Agastamento is displeasure or irritation here, and exte-rior retains the printed physical word division.
Fuzen means not good, glossed zen ni arazu: initial I in Ien has consonantal J value. Fuzen no tomogara refers to people lacking virtue, not to an otherwise puzzling ien noun.

runs.text: Os que não ſão virtuoſos, ou os maos.

lines.note: Those who are not virtuous, or the bad, completes the definition of fuzen no tomogara. The beginning ra belongs to tomoga-ra on the preceding line.
Fūzen means before the wind, kaze no mae. The example prints Fujenno without repeating the headword's accent; preserve that actual omission rather than harmonizing the two forms.

Fūzen no tomoshibi wa kie yasushi says a lamp exposed to wind goes out easily. The Japanese example and Portuguese gloss both continue naturally, with the gloss carried onto the next page; the bottom catchword is separate furniture.
